Recipes for Choosing a Learning Target

Rules of thumb for a reinforcement learning target: freeze, take a second estimate, or take the minimum, and why the combinations table is one reading, not a law.

October 17, 20265 min readUpdated October 27, 2026

reinforcement-learningmachine-learning

Every Q-learning update moves an estimate toward a number called the learning target. The annoying part is that we build that number out of the same estimates we are trying to fix. Picture the next state: two actions, Left and Right, both truly worth 10. The live network guesses Left 14 and Right 9, so it picks Left, and it picks Left because of the +4 error. Ask the same network what Left is worth and it says 14. We just trained toward a number that is too high for the exact reason it got picked.

So who should do the scoring? I find it more useful to ask two questions about any candidate: how often does it change, and how much of the chooser's error does it share? The top of the board scores that same Left pick four ways. Then there is a second problem that no choice of scorer touches. Say the rewards over three steps are 0, 0 and then 4. After the first zero, do we trust the network's guess about what comes next, or wait until we actually see the 4? Trusting the guess risks inheriting its bias. Waiting for every real reward is honest, but over a long episode the noise piles up. Generalized advantage estimation (GAE) puts a dial between the two: it adds up the one-step prediction errors along the way and lets each later one fade by a factor λ. The bottom of the board runs it.

Look at the error column first. The live network grades its own pick at 14 and carries the full +4. For this fixed next state and Left pick, the frozen score stays at 13 until the next refresh, and it keeps its +3 error, because the copy learned from the same history: stable, and still wrong. A separate scorer helps when its error on the picked action lines up less with the chooser's; here the second estimate lands at 9, off by −1 instead of +4. The minimum keeps the lower estimate: it can offset overestimation and deepen underestimation. So does letting the live network choose actually help? In one small CartPole comparison with frozen scoring, the frozen chooser averaged 159.1 and the live chooser averaged 147.5. That is three seeds each, with standard errors of 5.2 and 22.0, so I would not call a winner from it.

Back to the bottom panel. Our weighted sum is 0.25: a small positive signal that the first action did better than V(s₀) predicted. PPO uses this signal to encourage the action, and a negative one would discourage it. PPO then clips its training objective, so making an action much more likely stops earning extra credit. That clipping is a separate step from computing the advantage, and it puts no hard cap on how far the policy moves. For λ, ask which source you trust less: small λ leans on the value estimate, and large λ leans on later rewards, which can be noisy. I pick every target here the same way. Each recipe trades one error for another, so choose the one you can live with: a stale estimate, shared selection error, downward bias, or reward noise.

GAE endpoints, cut-off rollouts and what λ = 0.95 means

The TD error is δ_t = r_t + γV(s_{t+1}) − V(s_t) and GAE sums A_t = δ_t + γλδ_{t+1} + (γλ)^2δ_{t+2} + …, so the weight at offset k is (γλ)^k (Schulman et al., §3, equations 16–18). At λ = 0 you get the one-step estimate δ_t. At λ = 1 you get the discounted return minus V(s_t) when the episode really ends. If a rollout is cut off at step H before the episode ends, keep the bootstrap value V(s_H) at the cut and stop the trace at a reset.

People often read λ = 0.95 as a 95% full-return, 5% one-step mix. It is a decay rate. With γ = 1, successive weights are 0.95, 0.95². In general they are γ × 0.95, (γ × 0.95)².

Where the Left and Right numbers come from

The Left and Right values are invented to show the mechanism. They have no units and they come from no measurement. The live network does the choosing, so the second estimate's own favorite (Right, 11) never enters this target. To choose with one estimate and score with another is the idea behind Double Q-learning. The two estimates can still end up correlated.

Methods and the CartPole comparison

Frozen scoring is the target network from DQN. Double DQN lets the live network choose and the frozen copy score, so the two still share a learning history. The minimum is the clipped estimate in TD3. The CartPole numbers come from the Breaking Bellman combinations table: one environment, one settings row and three seeds. The ± is the standard error across those seeds. It does not measure how much the target moves.
